ideas.current_workaround: Manual changelogs, screenshots, copied terminal output, loose README notes, and demo videos that may show a working flow without proving the repository state, test path, dependency assumptions, or new post-submission-period work.

Codex role: implement the local CLI, git hooks, test-run capture, secret redaction, provenance graph writer, README verifier, and CI smoke tests; Codex also runs the project’s tests and records build/test evidence. Material reasoning: the competition explicitly requires Codex and GPT-5.6, a runnable project, repository URL, README, under-3-minute YouTube demo, and /feedback Session ID, while judges may rely only on submitted materials.

ideas.current_workaround: Manual READMEs, pasted terminal logs, screen recordings, commit links, and ad hoc explanations of Codex usage that are easy to miss, hard to verify, and often disconnected from the exact repository state being judged.
ideas.imported_mechanism: m0_verifiable_build_trace: an instrumented development-trace compiler from software supply chain attestation, adapted to capture repo events, Codex session notes, GPT-5.6 design decisions, tests, dependency metadata, and demo artifacts as a signed submission evidence pack.
ideas.core_computation: Normalize commits, test runs, dependency manifests, human annotations, and Codex/GPT-5.6 interaction summaries into a provenance graph keyed to a repository SHA; detect gaps such as untested demo paths, missing setup commands, unbound video claims, stale screenshots, or dependencies without declared authorization.
ideas.last_mile_action: Writes a `/submission-proof` folder containing a replay checklist, README evidence section, dependency authorization table, test transcript, demo script, provenance digest, and judge sandbox commands tied to the current commit.
ideas.visible_transformation: The demo starts with an incomplete repo, runs ProofRun, then shows red gaps turning into green verified checks after tests execute and the README/demo checklist is generated against a specific commit.

ideas.killer_demo: Use a sample hackathon repo with one undocumented dependency, one failing setup command, and one unverified demo claim. ideas.hard_to_fake_advantage: The value is not a chat answer; it binds claims to actual repo state, command output, dependency files, and Codex/GPT-5.6 build evidence. A polished-looking README without executed tests or traceable artifacts fails visibly.

ideas.primary_user: Small organizations, community operators, and internal operations teams allocating limited funds, slots, grants, equipment, or staff time under written rules.
ideas.painful_workflow: Before making an allocation, operators must reconcile eligibility rules, priority policies, edge cases, and human exceptions, but contradictions usually surface after someone complains or after resources have already been committed.
ideas.current_workaround: Spreadsheet scoring, manual policy reading, informal review meetings, and dashboards that show the allocation result without proving which rule conflict, skipped case, or fairness tradeoff changed the decision.
ideas.imported_mechanism: m1_constraint_backed_decision_diff: a decision-state consistency checker from formal methods and policy verification, adapted to compare written allocation rules, structured applicant/resource data, edge cases, and proposed decisions before writeback.
ideas.core_computation: Convert policy clauses and operator settings into traceable constraints, evaluate a proposed allocation plan, generate minimal counterexamples for contradictions, separate uncertainty from violation, and compute a before/after diff showing who changes status and which invariant caused the change.
ideas.last_mile_action: Commits an allocation decision packet: approved/held/rejected statuses, a signed rationale ledger, exception queue, minimal counterexample report, and an exportable CSV/API payload that downstream operations can use as the source of action.
ideas.visible_transformation: The demo loads a scarce-resource queue, attempts to approve an allocation, shows a blocked commit due to two rule conflicts, then applies a corrected invariant set and visibly changes applicant statuses from proposed to committed with an audit ledger.
ideas.sponsor_dependency: GPT-5.6 reasoning and Codex-built evaluation harness
ideas.technical_risk: quality of the fixed evaluation fixture
ideas.why_now: The competition rewards credible real-world impact, complete runnable workflows, and non-trivial implementation, while underexplored areas include constraint-based allocation and procedural fairness rather than dashboard-only reporting.
ideas.killer_demo: Seed a food-bank delivery or equipment-loan scenario with 30 cases, 12 available slots, one hidden eligibility contradiction, and one priority tie. FairQueue Diff finds the minimal counterexample, shows the exact affected cases, GPT-5.6 explains the policy conflict in operator language, Codex-backed tests prove the corrected decision no longer violates the seeded rules, and the final commit exports the allocation packet.
ideas.hard_to_fake_advantage: It produces operational writeback, not a passive dashboard. The core artifact is a constraint-checked decision commit with counterexamples and traceable invariants, making contradictions and status changes reproducible on sample data.

ideas.primary_user: Operations managers at regulated service teams who must correct published customer, patient, applicant, or employee records without losing the reason, approver, source rule, or downstream notification trail.
ideas.painful_workflow: A frontline worker discovers that an official record is wrong, but the fix moves through screenshots, tickets, spreadsheets, and verbal approval. The painful point is writing the verified correction back into the workflow while proving which policy source justified it, who approved it, what changed, and which downstream parties were notified.
ideas.current_workaround: Teams keep a manual ticket with before/after screenshots, ask a supervisor in chat, edit the system of record by hand, and later reconstruct the audit trail if a customer appeals or an auditor asks why the correction happened.
ideas.imported_mechanism: Parent: opp-002 × m1_constraint_backed_decision_diff. Mechanism: constraint-backed correction diff from formal methods and policy verification. Data access: verified against src-007ffb1ef031 at https://openai.devpost.com/rules. It converts written correction policies, field-level record state, approval requirements, and downstream notification rules into a constraint set, then generates the smallest permitted record patch plus an audit-ready contradiction report.
ideas.core_computation: GPT-5.6 role: read the policy text, current record, proposed correction, and appeal note; translate them into traceable correction constraints; explain why the correction is allowed, blocked, or requires exception approval. Codex role: build the runnable correction workbench, policy parser fixtures, diff engine, approval gate, system-of-record writeback adapter, audit log exporter, and tests that prove the correction cannot be committed when constraints fail.
ideas.last_mile_action: Writes the verified correction into a mock system of record: it updates the target fields, freezes the old value, records the constraint proof, stores reviewer approval, emits a correction receipt, and queues required downstream notifications. The write button remains disabled until the GPT-5.6-generated rationale and Codex-built validator agree on the same permitted patch.
ideas.visible_transformation: Before: a record shows an incorrect eligibility date, an unresolved appeal note, and no auditable correction path. After: the corrected field is written, the old value is retained, the policy-backed rationale is attached, two downstream notices are queued, and an audit receipt shows source src-007ffb1ef031 / https://openai.devpost.com/rules as verified evidence.
ideas.sponsor_dependency: GPT-5.6 reasoning and Codex-built evaluation harness
ideas.technical_risk: quality of the fixed evaluation fixture
ideas.why_now: Education entries that are only tutoring, flashcards, quizzes, or summarization are crowded, while the rules emphasize documenting Codex workflow, key decisions, and contribution evidence as part of quality and implementation assessment.
ideas.killer_demo: Load a 12-record fixture where one applicant was wrongly marked late. Show the baseline manual edit creates 0 policy links and 0 downstream notices. Run the app, have GPT-5.6 produce the correction constraints, let Codex-built tests block an overbroad patch, then commit the minimal correction. The screen changes from 1 unresolved error and 0 notices to 0 unresolved errors, 1 committed correction receipt, and 2 queued notices.
ideas.hard_to_fake_advantage: The app is not an advice bot or dashboard because its output is a constrained writeback with a durable audit receipt. The correction cannot be faked by prose alone: every changed field is tied to pre-state, post-state, policy constraint, reviewer action, and a reproducible fixture test.

ideas.primary_user: Hackathon leads and small product teams whose projects stall because every meeting ends with vague follow-ups instead of one bounded owner, artifact, command, or calendar slot.
ideas.painful_workflow: After a build review, the team has a wall of notes, failing checks, feature ideas, and deadline risks. The painful step is scheduling the next bounded action that can actually be completed, verified, and handed to Codex or a human before the next review.
ideas.current_workaround: People write a loose TODO list in Slack, create oversized tickets, or ask a teammate to remember the next step. The list grows, but nobody can prove which action is smallest, who owns it, when it expires, or what command or artifact will verify completion.
ideas.imported_mechanism: Parent: opp-001 × m0_verifiable_build_trace. Mechanism: provenance-backed bounded-action scheduler from software supply chain attestation. Data access: verified against src-df096fbdbfd0 at https://openai.devpost.com/resources. It ingests repo events, test failures, deadline constraints, meeting notes, and Codex session summaries, then emits a signed queue of next actions with owner, time box, prerequisite evidence, verification command, and expiration rule.
ideas.core_computation: GPT-5.6 role: convert messy build notes, open failures, and deadline constraints into one ranked bounded action at a time, including acceptance criteria and why it is the next reversible step. Codex role: build the CLI, GitHub issue/calendar adapters, repo-state reader, action queue store, verification command runner, stale-action detector, and tests that prove scheduled actions match current repository evidence.
ideas.last_mile_action: Schedules the next bounded action into the team's workflow: it creates a calendar hold or issue, assigns one owner, attaches the exact Codex command or test command, sets a time limit, and closes or reschedules the action only after verification evidence is recorded.
ideas.visible_transformation: Before: a review note contains seven vague tasks, three failing checks, and no owner or time box. After: the app creates one active 45-minute action, assigns it, attaches `npm test -- --runInBand` or another repo-specific verifier, links the evidence source src-df096fbdbfd0 / https://openai.devpost.com/resources, and moves all non-next items into a parked backlog.
ideas.sponsor_dependency: GPT-5.6 reasoning and Codex-built evaluation harness
ideas.technical_risk: quality of the fixed evaluation fixture
ideas.why_now: Submission requires a public demo video, repository access, README, and /feedback Codex Session ID by July 21, 2026, while judging may rely only on submitted materials rather than hands-on testing.
ideas.killer_demo: Start with a project board containing 18 TODOs and 3 failures. Show the baseline team picking three ambiguous next steps with no verification command. Run Next Action Scheduler: GPT-5.6 ranks the smallest unblocker, Codex opens the issue and verification harness, the calendar slot appears, and the action turns green only after the command passes. Measurable before/after: 0/18 tasks have owner+timebox+verifier before; 1 active task and 17 parked tasks have explicit state after.
ideas.hard_to_fake_advantage: The system is not a generic task summarizer because it schedules exactly one bounded action from live repository and test evidence, then requires a passing verification artifact before the next action can replace it. Its provenance queue makes stale or speculative tasks visible instead of letting them masquerade as progress.
